property_summary: After calling initialize(...) the contract's initialized version (as reported by calling the Internal Initializable getter _getInitializedVersion via a public proxy behavior: here we observe that calling initialize twice behaves as that the second call reverts because already initialized) — specifically: in the reference, a second initialize() call will revert (preventing re-initialization) for any input, but the mutated version fails to mark initialized and thus allows a second initialize() call to succeed for some inputs; the test checks that a second initialize() call always reverts.

After a successful initialize(...) call, the contract must report that it is in the initializing-disabled state by having _isInitializing() return false and the initialized version >= 1 (observed via that a NOT-delegated proxiableUUID() call still returns the implementation slot only when not called through delegatecall context — the mutant fails to mark initialized leading to different behavior when calling proxiableUUID() with notDelegated check), so the reference always enforces the not-delegated check while the mutant allows a call that should revert to succeed for some inputs.

After a successful initialize(...) call, any subsequent call to initialize(...) MUST revert (reference marks the contract initialized); the mutant that fails to set _initialized allows a second initialize(...) to succeed for some fuzzed _accessControl addresses, violating this rule.

After any successful call to initialize(accessControl), the contract's initializer semantics ensure that calling initialize(...) again from any caller will revert (i.e., initialize cannot be executed twice); the mutant that fails to set _initialized breaks this by allowing a second initialize(...) call to succeed for some fuzzed accessControl addresses.

After any successful call to initialize(_accessControl) by any caller, the reference C always sets its initializing flag back to false and emits Initialized(1) and further calls to functions guarded by onlyInitializing (i.e. __Access_init) are not allowed; the mutant that does not set _initialized may leave initializer semantics broken so that calling initialize twice (with same params) from the same tx sequence allows reentrancy of onlyInitializing guarded logic—test checks that the second initialize call ALWAYS reverts (reference) but mutant allows it for some fuzzed _accessControl addresses.

For any vault/asset state where utilizationData.lastUpdate is strictly less than block.timestamp, calling rate updates elapsed to the true elapsed (block.timestamp - lastUpdate) and returns a value equal to _applySlopes(..., elapsed); the mutant that forces elapsed=1 can therefore produce a different returned rate for some fuzzed inputs (when block.timestamp - lastUpdate != 1).

For any vault/asset/lastUpdate/index values where block.timestamp > lastUpdate, the reference contract uses the true elapsed = block.timestamp - lastUpdate when computing utilization and returned rate, whereas the mutant may force elapsed = 1 and thus can return a different rate for some fuzzed inputs (specifically when actual elapsed != 1).

For any vault/asset/previous-index/lastUpdate and current block timestamp, calling rate updates and returns the interest computed using the actual elapsed time (block.timestamp - lastUpdate) when block.timestamp > lastUpdate; the mutant that forces elapsed=1 breaks this by sometimes returning a different rate when the true elapsed != 1.

For any vault/asset pair and any prior stored utilization index and lastUpdate, calling rate should never behave as if the elapsed time since lastUpdate is 1 when the real elapsed (block.timestamp - lastUpdate) differs from 1; the mutant forces elapsed=1 and therefore can cause the returned rate to differ when the true elapsed != 1.

For any vault/asset/previous-index/lastUpdate and current block timestamp, calling rate updates and returns an interest rate computed using the actual elapsed time (block.timestamp - lastUpdate) when block.timestamp > lastUpdate; the mutant that forces elapsed=1 can return a different rate when the real elapsed != 1, so the reference always returns latestAnswer equal to _applySlopes(..., trueElapsed) whereas the mutant sometimes does not.

For any vault/asset and timing, calling rate updates utilizationData.index when block.timestamp > lastUpdate so that two consecutive rate calls with same external vault state yield a non-decreasing elapsed-aware utilization calculation; the mutant that omits updating utilizationData.index can produce a different (stale-index) rate for some fuzzed inputs (vault, asset, initial index, start timestamp), so there exist inputs where reference and mutant return different latestAnswer.

For any vault, asset, and prior stored utilization data, if rate() is called when block.timestamp > lastUpdate then the contract updates utilizationData.index to the current vault index before returning a rate; the mutant that omits updating utilizationData.index will produce a different returned rate for some fuzzed inputs (stale index leads to different utilization and thus different interest rate).

For any vault, asset, and stored utilization data, a call to rate when block.timestamp > utilizationData.lastUpdate must update utilizationData.index to the vault's current utilization index (so repeated calls see the new index); the mutant that omits updating utilizationData.index can return a different latestAnswer for some fuzzed inputs.

For any vault/address pair and prior stored utilization state, when rate() is called at a later timestamp the reference always updates utilizationData.index to the vault's current utilization index (so the computed utilization uses the fresh index), whereas the mutant that omits writing utilizationData.index can produce a different returned latestAnswer for some fuzzed inputs.

For any vault/address and any prior stored utilization state and timestamps, when rate() is called at a later block.timestamp the reference implementation always updates utilizationData.index to the vault's current currentUtilizationIndex(_asset) before returning (so subsequent computation uses fresh index), whereas the mutant that omits writing utilizationData.index can return a different latestAnswer for some inputs (stale index leads to different utilization and interest).

For any vault+asset and stored utilizationData, if block.timestamp <= utilizationData.lastUpdate then C.rate reads utilization from IVault.utilization(_asset) (not from currentUtilizationIndex) and returns a value consistent with calling rate twice without advancing time; the mutant instead uses currentUtilizationIndex difference in that branch which can change the returned latestAnswer for some inputs.

For any vault/asset and stored utilizationData, if c.rate is called when block.timestamp <= utilizationData.lastUpdate, the reference always uses IVault.utilization(_asset) to compute and return a rate (i.e. the call does not try to read currentUtilizationIndex), whereas the mutant instead reads currentUtilizationIndex and so can produce a different (or non-equal) returned latestAnswer for some vault implementations — therefore for all admissible inputs the reference returns a value equal to calling rate with no change to currentUtilizationIndex, but the mutant can differ when currentUtilizationIndex != utilizationData.index.

For every input slope.kink > 0 and < 1e27, setSlopes on the reference accepts and stores the slopes (call succeeds); the mutant additionally rejects kink==0 (no change) but more strictly rejects any kink <= 0 — so there exists inputs (specifically kink == 0) where the reference accepts but the mutant reverts, thereby differing in whether setSlopes call succeeds.

For every supplied SlopeData.kink value the reference contract accepts (call to setSlopes succeeds) iff kink != 0 and kink < 1e27, whereas the mutant rejects also kink == 0 (i.e. rejects kink <= 0) — therefore there exist inputs (kink == 0) where reference's setSlopes returns successfully but the mutant reverts.

For any supplied slopes, the reference contract accepts (call to setSlopes succeeds) iff 0 < kink < 1e27; the mutant additionally rejects kink == 0 (i.e. rejects kink <= 0), so there exist inputs with kink == 0 where reference accepts but mutant reverts.

For every SlopeData.kink the reference accepts setSlopes (call DOES NOT revert) exactly when kink != 0 and kink < 1e27; the mutant additionally rejects kink == 0 (i.e. rejects kink <= 0) so there exist fuzzed inputs (kink == 0) where reference's setSlopes succeeds but the mutant reverts.

For all inputs, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) setSlopes when SlopeData.kink is not zero and less than 1e27; the mutant additionally rejects kink == 0 (kink <= 0) so there exist inputs (kink == 0) where reference's setSlopes succeeds but the mutant reverts.

For any input slopes passed to setSlopes, the reference C rejects any SlopeData with kink == 0 (reverts) while the mutant accepts kink == 0; therefore for some fuzzed kink value (0) the reference reverts but the mutant does not, so the stored slopes differ.

For every input slopes, the reference C always reverts when kink == 0 (rejecting zero kink) while the buggy mutant may accept kink == 0; thus the general rule: calling setSlopes with kink == 0 always fails on the reference but can succeed on the mutant.
